iterations.hypothesis: The organizers' FM baseline, ported to the DataAPI. The incumbent every candidate is measured against.

The FM baseline is trained with pointwise logloss, which optimizes each impression's absolute calibrated probability independently — but the metric only ever compares scores *within* a user's group, and any monotone shift that is common to a whole group cancels out of both GAUC and nDCG@5 (exactly the mechanism the ledger already confirmed for user-side constants). Pointwise logloss spends most of its gradient budget getting absolute probabilities right across users, which the ranking metric never rewards. Replacing it with a per-user listwise softmax cross-entropy (target = label mass, i.e. `y_i / sum(y)` inside each user's group, softmax over the group's raw scores) puts every gradient step directly on the within-group ordering that GAUC/nDCG@5 actually score, using the exact same FM scoring function and features. This is a pure loss change (organizers' axis 1, rated most likely to help) with no new features or parameters, so any improvement is attributable to the objective-metric mismatch closing, not to capacity or leakage. I expect a modest but real gain, mainly on nDCG@5 since the loss is now literally optimizing a softmax proxy for top-of-list mass; I predict primary +0.006.
iterations.grounding: within_user_variance (ranking is scored strictly inside a user's group, so any loss term that only moves group-constant calibration is wasted; a listwise loss over exactly the impression group removes that waste)
iterations.change_summary: Replaced pointwise logloss training with a within-user listwise softmax cross-entropy (target = normalized label mass per group), same FM architecture/features/optimizer otherwise.

iterations.hypothesis: The FM baseline scores every (user,video) pair through a single static user embedding, so a user's history only enters via that one learned vector — it never expresses "this candidate resembles what I actually liked before," a signal that varies *by candidate* and therefore is not cancelled by within-user normalization (unlike pure user-side bias, which the ledger already proved contributes exactly zero). The measured history depth (median 31, mean 43.5 impressions per user in train) is enough to build a per-user "liked-item profile": the mean FM item-embedding of videos that user long-viewed in train. Scoring a candidate by its dot-product with that profile is a lightweight target-attention/SVD++-style sequence signal — it varies within a user's impression group because different candidate videos have different embeddings, so the dot product differs row to row, unlike a user-only bias term. I predict this adds real but modest lift, mostly to nDCG@5 for users with informative history, and roughly zero for users with no positives in train (~5.1%) or unseen users (~1.6-3.6%), whose profile vector is zero and who fall back to the plain FM score. iterations.hypothesis: The baseline trains with pointwise logistic loss, whose per-row gradient sigmoid(z)-y is driven by absolute label frequency and therefore feeds the bias `b` and the first-order weight `W[user_id]` — both of which are constant inside a user's impression group and provably cancel out of within-user ranking (already confirmed exactly by the user_side_first_order_terms dead end). Every gradient step spends part of its Adam budget calibrating this discarded component instead of sharpening the cross terms (`user_id × item-side`) that actually move rank order. GAUC is literally Mann-Whitney pairwise AUC, so replacing the pointwise loss with a **pairwise BPR loss sampled within each user's positive/negative pairs** should align training directly with what is scored: for a pair (i,j) from the same user, the loss depends only on z_i − z_j, so any term shared identically by i and j (the global bias b, and — critically — the user's own first-order weight/embedding contribution that doesn't interact with the item side) receives *exactly zero gradient by construction*, algebraically forcing all learning capacity into the item-varying interaction terms. This differs mechanistically from the already-discarded listwise softmax (which normalizes over a whole variable-size group and can suffer high-variance gradients on the large fraction of small/skewed groups); BPR's pairwise formulation is simpler, lower-variance, and matches GAUC's own pairwise definition term-for-term, so I expect it to recover most of what listwise lost and add a genuine, mechanism-explainable gain on top of the pointwise baseline.
iterations.grounding: within_user_variance / user_side_first_order_terms (constant-in-group terms provably cancel; GAUC's own definition is pairwise Mann-Whitney U, which BPR directly targets)
iterations.change_summary: Replaced pointwise logistic FM training with a pairwise BPR loss sampled from each user's (positive, negative) impression pairs, so gradient to group-constant terms (bias, user first-order weight) is analytically zero and all capacity goes to item-interacting terms that actually determine within-user order.

iterations.hypothesis: The current objective is pointwise BCE averaged over rows, which gives every training row equal weight. Since `train_history_per_user` shows impressions/user ranging from p10=5 to p90=97 (mean 43.5), this implicitly weights the loss by each user's activity level: a 97-impression user contributes ~20x more gradient mass than a 5-impression user. But the evaluation metric does the opposite of that: nDCG@5 averages one score per user regardless of group size, and GAUC (per the frozen `evaluate.py`) weights only by positive count among discriminative users, not by row count. So the objective is over-fitting the ordering preferences of heavy-impression users at the expense of the light-impression users the metric actually weights equally -- a group-size mismatch that is invisible in the loss curve but directly costs ranking quality on the sparse-impression test population (test p50=5, 13.6% of users have <=1 impression). The fix: reweight each training row by 1/(that user's impression count in the training batch), renormalized to preserve the overall gradient scale, so every user contributes equally to the loss the way nDCG@5 scores them equally. This changes only the training weighting scheme, not the model or features, isolating the mechanism cleanly.
